scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): strongly backs questioning but argues 'always' is too absolute, since some foundations must be accepted first; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose at about 400 words on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: Real education teaches people not just to memorise facts but to think for themselves.
Some people argue that students should always question what they are taught instead of accepting it passively.
I strongly agree that questioning is essential, but I believe the word always goes too far, since some knowledge must be accepted before it can be questioned wisely.
First, questioning what we are taught lies at the very heart of real learning.
Students who ask why and how understand ideas far more deeply than those who merely repeat them.
For example, science itself advances only because researchers refuse to accept old answers and keep testing them.
This shows that active questioning turns passive listeners into genuine, independent thinkers.
A student who never questions is easily misled and may absorb errors or even harmful ideas without resistance.
Questioning also keeps teachers honest and pushes human knowledge itself to improve over time.
For these reasons, a habit of thoughtful questioning is one of the greatest gifts of an education.

sections.role: Body 2 — Why some acceptance is needed

sentences.text: Second, however, the demand that students question everything at all times is unrealistic and even unwise.
Before anyone can question an idea intelligently, she must first understand the basic facts on which it rests.
Consider a beginner in mathematics who must accept the rules of arithmetic before she can challenge anything more advanced.
Trying to question every basic fact from the start would leave a student confused and unable to build any real knowledge.
Some foundations must be learned and trusted first, so that later questioning has something solid to stand on.
Endless doubt about everything can also become its own kind of trap, leading to confusion rather than understanding.
Wise questioning, then, grows out of knowledge rather than replacing it entirely.
In conclusion, students should certainly be encouraged to question what they are taught.
But they cannot question everything at once, since thoughtful doubt depends on first understanding the basics.
The ideal student learns the foundations carefully and then questions them boldly, rather than doing only one or the other.
